item.title: [infoq] 多个 AI 智能体“同住”一台 EC2：AgentCore 推出持久计算
item.description: AWS announced runtime instances for Bedrock AgentCore, which run agents on managed EC2 instances inside the customer's account while preserving the existing AgentCore API, identity, and observability. Sessions can last up to 14 days (vs. the 8-hour microVM cap), with shared file systems, GPU-backed instances, and support for frameworks like CrewAI and LangGraph. It targets teams whose agents need longer than 8 hours and benefit from multiple agents collaborating on one host.

It targets the bottleneck between AI-accelerated code generation and limited human review while preserving existing branch protection, review, and merge workflows. Teams can adopt stacked development without third-party tools.

item.title: [infoq] Next.js 16.3 发布：即时导航、开发内存最高降低 90%，构建速度大幅提升
item.description: Vercel shipped Next.js 16.3, focused on developer experience: Turbopack's disk cache and new memory reclamation cut `next dev` memory usage by up to 90%, and repeated CI builds run up to 5.5x faster. The release introduces the optional Instant Navigations toolkit, built on the `use cache` directive and enabled via two config flags, bringing SPA-like speed to the server-side model. Server rendering now uses native Node.js streams, and the edge runtime is deprecated.

item.title: [infoq] Cloudflare 将 CI 管道转变为 TypeScript 工作流
item.description: Cloudflare shipped @cloudflare/ci, a CI SDK that lets developers define pipelines in TypeScript instead of YAML, running each step as a durable Workflow on the Workers runtime. Steps execute in isolated sandboxes with checkpointing, so failed steps retry in place and resume from that step, and dependency caching stores install snapshots in R2. It's a platform-level take on CI, wiring together Workflows, sandboxes, containers, Durable Objects, and R2 rather than a drop-in replacement.

item.title: [hackernews] MS Paint and Photos inivisibly watermark even locally generated output with GUID
item.description: A reverse-engineering look shows that Microsoft Paint and Photos embed a server-issued GUID into the pixels of AI images produced locally, forming an invisible watermark. Local generation therefore doesn't guarantee an untraceable file. The finding matters for privacy-conscious users and for anyone researching AI-content provenance, though only the mechanism has been confirmed so far.
